text: summary MAVLink is the language the flight controller uses to talk to the ground control station, the companion computer, telemetry and your scripts. Everything you did in SITL via pymavlink is MAVLink. This module takes the protocol apart at a level sufficient to write your own clients: the packet structure, system and component, heartbeat, commands with acknowledgment, parameters, telemetry streams. Two tools to choose from: pymavlink low level, everything is visible and MAVSDK a high-level API . theory The packet MAVLink 2 is a binary protocol over UART, UDP or TCP. The packet: the start byte 0xFD , length, flags, sequence number, system_id , component_id , a three-byte message ID, the payload, CRC. The checksum includes a “salt” from the message definition, so both sides must use identical definitions the dialect . Messages are described in XML: common.xml holds the common ones, ardupilotmega.xml the ArduPilot extensions. Libraries for C, Python and other languages are generated from the XML. System and component system_id is the vehicle 1 by default , component_id is what's inside: the autopilot 1 , a camera, a gimbal, the companion computer. The GCS is usually system 255. Commands are addressed to a system+component pair; the companion computer is a separate component of the same system. Heartbeat HEARTBEAT ID 0 once a second from every participant: vehicle type, autopilot, mode, arm state. No heartbeat, no link — that's why every client starts with wait_heartbeat . No heartbeat from the GCS for longer than the timeout is a GCS failsafe. The main messages - Telemetry from the vehicle: SYS_STATUS 1 , ATTITUDE 30 , GLOBAL_POSITION_INT 33 , RC_CHANNELS 65 , BATTERY_STATUS 147 , STATUSTEXT 253 — text messages, including pre-arm ones . - Commands: COMMAND_LONG 76 with a MAV_CMD_ code and seven parameters; the reply is COMMAND_ACK 77 with the result. Example codes: MAV_CMD_COMPONENT_ARM_DISARM 400 , MAV_CMD_NAV_TAKEOFF 22 , MAV_CMD_DO_SET_MODE 176 . - Stream rates: MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL 511 — request a specific message at the interval you need; MAV_CMD_REQUEST_MESSAGE 512 — once. - Parameters: PARAM_REQUEST_READ 20 → PARAM_VALUE 22 ; writing is PARAM_SET 23 , confirmed by the same PARAM_VALUE . - Control in GUIDED: SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED 84 and SET_POSITION_TARGET_GLOBAL_INT 86 — a position or velocity target; the basis of offboard control from a companion. - Missions: MISSION_COUNT 44 , MISSION_ITEM_INT 73 , MISSION_REQUEST_INT 51 , MISSION_ACK 47 — the dialog from the missions module. The acknowledgment rule A command without a COMMAND_ACK check is hope, not control. The result MAV_RESULT_ACCEPTED 0 means “accepted”; the other codes are a refusal, and its reason usually arrives in STATUSTEXT . pymavlink vs MAVSDK - pymavlink is a thin wrapper over the protocol: you see every message; it suits learning, diagnostics and non-standard things. The code is verbose. - MAVSDK C++, Python offers high-level actions: arm , takeoff , goto_location , telemetry subscriptions. Faster for writing applications, less visible from the inside. Historically closer to PX4, but works with ArduPilot. The MAVLink 2 frame byte by byte FD len incompat_flags compat_flags seq sysid compid msgid 3 payload len crc 2 signature 13 . incompat_flags bit 0 means the packet is signed; the signature is the first 48 bits of SHA-256 over secret key + header + payload + CRC + link_id + timestamp , not HMAC protection against command spoofing over an open radio channel — the key is set in Mission Planner/QGC and sent to the autopilot with the SETUP_SIGNING message . CRC-16/MCRF4XX over the frame + the message's CRC_EXTRA byte from the XML — a dialect mismatch = “silence”. The payload is compressed by truncating trailing zero bytes which is why len is smaller than the struct size . Parameters in PARAM_VALUE are always float 32-bit ; ArduPilot sends integers cast to float C cast , PX4 byte-wise; the value type is in param_type MAV_PARAM_TYPE , which is easy to trip over in pymavlink. {{diagram:mavlink2-frame The MAVLink 2 frame: header, system and component IDs, payload, CRC with CRC_EXTRA, optional signature.}} Telemetry streams: who sets the rate ArduPilot sends streams according to the port's SRx_ parameters SR2_EXTRA1 — ATTITUDE, SR2_POSITION — GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, SR2_RAW_SENS — RAW_IMU… in Hz; the modern way is MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL 511 from the client: the interval in µs −1 — off, 0 — default . PX4 uses MAV_x_MODE profiles Normal/Onboard/OSD… . A 921600 baud port carries ~90 KB/s: ATTITUDE at 50 Hz + position at 10 Hz + RAW_IMU at 50 Hz is about 10 KB/s, so there is headroom; at 57600 a radio modem anything above 5–10 Hz chokes. Worked example: a reliable command python def cmd m, command, params, retries=3, timeout=1.0 : """Send COMMAND_LONG and wait for a matching ACK; retry on timeout; raise on rejection.""" p = list params + 0 7 - len params for _ in range retries : m.mav.command_long_send m.target_system, m.target_component, command, 0, p t0 = time.time while time.time - t0 < timeout: ack = m.recv_match type="COMMAND_ACK", blocking=True, timeout=timeout if ack and ack.command == command: if ack.result == mavutil.mavlink.MAV_RESULT_ACCEPTED: return True if ack.result == mavutil.mavlink.MAV_RESULT_IN_PROGRESS: continue raise RuntimeError f"cmd {command} rejected: result {ack.result}" raise TimeoutError f"cmd {command}: no ACK" STATUSTEXT explains the refusal in parallel “PreArm: …” . MAVSDK does the same under the hood — but you need to understand what's inside to read a tlog during an analysis. practice Step 1. Listen to telemetry python from pymavlink import mavutil m = mavutil.mavlink_connection "tcp:127.0.0.1:5762" m.wait_heartbeat print f"system {m.target_system} component {m.target_component}" ask for ATTITUDE at 10 Hz interval in microseconds m.mav.command_long_send m.target_system, m.target_component, mavutil.mavlink.MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL, 0, mavutil.mavlink.MAVLINK_MSG_ID_ATTITUDE,

title: MAVLink internals: frame, CRC, dialects, signing
summary: In the comp-mavlink module MAVLink was “a library that sends messages.” Here it becomes a protocol you can read by eye in a hex dump. We take apart the v1 and v2 frames byte by byte, the sequence number and how to count losses with it, CRC-16/MCRF4XX and why a CRC_EXTRA byte is mixed into it, why MA
headings: The MAVLink 2 frame seq and losses CRC and CRC_EXTRA Payload zero truncation Field order on the wire Dialects and mavgen Packet signing Step 1. Decoder by hand Step 2. CRC_EXTRA by hand Step 3. Your own dialect Step 4. Losses from seq
text: summary In the comp-mavlink module MAVLink was “a library that sends messages.” Here it becomes a protocol you can read by eye in a hex dump. We take apart the v1 and v2 frames byte by byte, the sequence number and how to count losses with it, CRC-16/MCRF4XX and why a CRC_EXTRA byte is mixed into it, why MAVLink 2 truncates trailing zeros in the payload and what that breaks in homemade parsers. Then — where messages come from: XML dialects, mavgen , field order on the wire not the one in the XML , extension fields and compatibility. The last part is packet signing: what the 13 bytes consist of, how the key gets into the autopilot, and what signing protects against and what it doesn't. Lab: a frame decoder without the pymavlink parser, your own dialect with a new message, automated tests in examples/mavlink/ . theory The MAVLink 2 frame Byte Field Meaning --- --- --- 0 STX = 0xFD start of frame v1 — 0xFE 1 len payload length after zero truncation 0–255 2 incompat_flags bit 0 — frame is signed; unknown bit → frame is dropped 3 compat_flags an unknown bit can be ignored 4 seq sequence number 0–255 from this sender 5 sysid sending system 6 compid sending component 7–9 msgid 24 bits, little-endian 10… payload len bytes +2 checksum CRC-16/MCRF4XX, little-endian +13 signature only if incompat_flags & 1 The v2 header is 10 bytes, v1 is 6 no flags, msgid is 1 byte, i.e. only messages with ID < 256 . All multi-byte numbers are little-endian. The minimum v2 frame is 12 bytes, the maximum is 280. {{diagram:mavlink2-frame MAVLink 2 frame: a 10-byte header, the payload, the CRC and an optional signature.}} seq and losses Each sender a sysid/compid pair increments seq modulo 256. A receiver that sees seq_new ≠ seq_old + 1 knows that seq_new − seq_old − 1 mod 256 frames were lost. That's exactly how QGC and Mission Planner compute “link quality” and the loss percentage — without any feedback from the radio. The trap: if one channel has two different senders with the same sysid/compid for example, two copies of the same script , the loss count becomes meaningless and routing becomes unpredictable. CRC and CRC_EXTRA The checksum is computed over all bytes after STX through the end of the payload header without STX + payload , using CRC-16/MCRF4XX polynomial 0x1021 in reflected form, initial value 0xFFFF; the check value for “123456789” is 0x6F91 . Then one more byte is “fed” into the CRC — CRC_EXTRA , computed from the message definition: its name and the list of fields with their types. It is not in the frame. Why: if the sender and receiver have different definitions for the same msgid a field was added, a type changed , the length may match but the meaning won't. CRC_EXTRA makes such frames invalid: the receiver silently drops them. Hence the classic symptom “the link is up, heartbeat is there, but this one message doesn't arrive” — the dialects diverged on one message. python def x25_crc data: bytes, crc: int = 0xFFFF - int: for b in data: tmp = b ^ crc & 0xFF tmp = tmp ^ tmp << 4 & 0xFF crc = crc 8 ^ tmp << 8 ^ tmp << 3 ^ tmp 4 & 0xFFFF return crc Payload zero truncation MAVLink 2 strips trailing zero bytes from the payload before sending: a COMMAND_LONG with param5–param7 = 0 goes out shorter than 33 bytes. The receiver must pad the payload with zeros to the full struct size before unpacking. A homemade parser that checks len == sizeof struct will drop half the messages, and it will look like “random losses.” At least one payload byte is always kept. Field order on the wire Fields in the XML are in an order convenient for humans. On the wire they are sorted by type size in descending order uint64/double → uint32/int32/float → uint16 → uint8/char , stable within the same size, and the extension fields after the <extensions/ tag go at the end in XML order. This way the struct is aligned without holes. In pymavlink this is ordered_fieldnames ; in the C headers — the field order in mavlink_ _t . CRC_EXTRA uses the fields in wire order, without extension fields: that's why adding an extension field doesn't break compatibility, while changing an old field does. Dialects and mavgen Messages are described in XML: minimal.xml HEARTBEAT, PROTOCOL_VERSION ⊂ standard.xml ⊂ common.xml ⊂ ardupilotmega.xml via <include . Your own dialect is an XML that includes common.xml , with your own messages in a dedicated ID range. mavgen generates a library from it: bash python -m pymavlink.tools.mavgen --lang=Python3 --wire-protocol=2.0 --output=mydialect.py mydialect.xml python -m pymavlink.tools.mavgen --lang=C --wire-protocol=2.0 --output=generated/ mydialect.xml Rules that save days of debugging: the msgid of a new message must not overlap existing ones; after changing the XML, rebuild all sides autopilot, companion, GCS ; check the generated CRC_EXTRA in both places. For experiments without rebuilding the autopilot there are ready-made generic messages: NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT 251 , NAMED_VALUE_INT 252 , DEBUG_VECT 250 , TUNNEL 385, arbitrary bytes with a payload type . Packet signing A signed frame incompat_flags bit 0 carries 13 bytes: link_id 1 , timestamp 6 bytes, unit — 10 µs since January 1, 2015 , signature the first 6 bytes of SHA-256 of “secret key + header + payload + CRC + link_id + timestamp” . The receiver checks the signature and that the timestamp is monotonic — this protects against both spoofing and replay of an intercepted frame. The key 32 bytes is passed to the autopilot with the SETUP_SIGNING message 256 over a trusted channel — usually USB; ArduPilot stores it in flash and on boot takes a timestamp one minute ahead of the last saved one. In Mission Planner — “Advanced → MAVLink Signing,” in QGC — the MAVLink settings. In ArduPilot 4.7+ bit 0 of the MAVn_OPTIONS parameter “Accept unsigned MAVLink2 messages” allows unsigned packets on a specific channel; in 4.6 and earlier there is no such setting — with signing enabled, unsigned packets are accepted only on channel 0 USB and for RADIO_STATUS . summary: MAVLink is not a set of messages but a set of **dialogues** (microservices): who starts, who replies, what to do on a loss. Almost every companion integration bug is a violation of one of these dialogues: a command sent without waiting for an ACK, a parameter “written” without an echo, a mission upl
headings: Heartbeat and state Commands: COMMAND_LONG, COMMAND_INT and ACK Parameters Missions: a dialogue driven by the receiver Telemetry streams Time MAVFTP, camera, gimbal, Remote ID Step 1. Tests without SITL Step 2. Your own mission client Step 3. In SITL Step 4. Parameters with encoding
text: summary MAVLink is not a set of messages but a set of dialogues microservices : who starts, who replies, what to do on a loss. Almost every companion integration bug is a violation of one of these dialogues: a command sent without waiting for an ACK, a parameter “written” without an echo, a mission uploaded halfway. This module goes through the main microservices: heartbeat and state, commands COMMAND_LONG / COMMAND_INT , ACK, IN_PROGRESS, the confirmation counter , parameters reading the list, writing with confirmation, type encoding , missions upload, download, partial update, geofences and rally points as separate mission types , telemetry stream control, MAVFTP, camera/gimbal and Remote ID — at the level of “which dialogue, and where it breaks.” Lab: a mission client with retries that passes the tests at 25 % packet loss. theory Heartbeat and state HEARTBEAT 0 once per second from every component: type MAV_TYPE , autopilot, base_mode the arm flag — MAV_MODE_FLAG_SAFETY_ARMED , custom_mode the mode number, different for each firmware , system_status . The heartbeat is participant discovery, the source of the address for routing, and the basis of failsafe: an autopilot that stops hearing the GCS heartbeat triggers the GCS failsafe if enabled ; a companion that stops hearing the autopilot must stop issuing setpoints. Rule: start any addressed commands only after the first heartbeat from the addressee. Commands: COMMAND_LONG, COMMAND_INT and ACK COMMAND_LONG 76 : target_system , target_component , command MAV_CMD , confirmation , seven float parameters. COMMAND_INT 75 : the same addressing and param1–4, but without the confirmation field instead there are current / autocontinue , unused ; parameters 5–6 are integers x , y latitude/longitude × 10⁷ without float precision loss and there is a frame field; it's preferred for commands with coordinates. The reply is COMMAND_ACK 77 with result : result Meaning What the client should do --- --- --- ACCEPTED 0 executed/accepted done TEMPORARILY_REJECTED 1 not possible right now retry later DENIED 2 forbidden in this state read STATUSTEXT, don't retry UNSUPPORTED 3 command not supported don't retry FAILED 4 attempted and failed investigate the cause IN_PROGRESS 5 long-running command, progress 0–100 wait for the final ACK The protocol prescribes: if no ACK arrives within the timeout, resend the command, incrementing confirmation . The receiver can use it to tell a retry from a new command. Without waiting for an ACK, a command is a hope; without a retry limit, it's a hang. {{diagram:mavlink-command-seq Command with acknowledgment: a retry when the ACK is lost, an intermediate IN_PROGRESS, the final result.}} Parameters - List: PARAM_REQUEST_LIST 21 → a stream of PARAM_VALUE 22 with param_count and param_index . Gaps are filled in by index via PARAM_REQUEST_READ 20 with param_index . - Reading one: PARAM_REQUEST_READ by name 16 characters, with no terminating null when the length is 16! or by index. - Writing: PARAM_SET 23 . There is no separate ACK — the confirmation is a PARAM_VALUE with the same name and the new value. If the echo comes back with the old value, the write was rejected out of range, read-only . - All values are sent in the float param_value field. ArduPilot sends integer types as a number cast to float C-cast , PX4 — bytewise the integer's bits in the float's bits . Which scheme the autopilot uses is reported by a flag in AUTOPILOT_VERSION.capabilities MAV_PROTOCOL_CAPABILITY_PARAM_ENCODE_C_CAST or ..._BYTEWISE . Getting the scheme wrong turns SYSID_THISMAV = 1 into 1.4e-45. For bulk parameter loading, so you don't run 1000 dialogues over the radio, there is MAVFTP: ArduPilot serves the whole @PARAM/param.pck file. Missions: a dialogue driven by the receiver Upload client → vehicle : 1. Client: MISSION_COUNT 44 with the number of items and mission_type . 2. The vehicle requests them one at a time: MISSION_REQUEST_INT 51 with seq . 3. The client replies with MISSION_ITEM_INT 73 with that seq . 4. After the last item the vehicle sends MISSION_ACK 47 with the result. The key idea: the receiving side holds the initiative . It requests the items, and it also re-sends the request on a timeout. The sender replies to every request, including repeated ones, and doesn't send items “ahead.” Download vehicle → client is symmetrical: MISSION_REQUEST_LIST → MISSION_COUNT → the client requests MISSION_REQUEST_INT → MISSION_ITEM_INT → the client finishes with MISSION_ACK . mission_type : 0 — route, 1 — geofence fence , 2 — rally points rally , 255 — all for clearing with MISSION_CLEAR_ALL . Item 0 in ArduPilot is the home position; uploading from item 1 in Mission Planner is just the UI, and on the wire home is still seq 0. Avoid the deprecated MISSION_ITEM 39 and MISSION_REQUEST 40 with float coordinates: float precision at a latitude is ~ a meter. In flight: MISSION_CURRENT 42 — the current item, MISSION_ITEM_REACHED 46 — reached, MAV_CMD_DO_SET_MISSION_CURRENT 224 — jump to the MISSION_SET_CURRENT 41 message has been deprecated since 2022 and replaced by this command . Partial update: MISSION_WRITE_PARTIAL_LIST 38 with an index range — not supported everywhere; it's more reliable to re-upload the whole thing and verify by downloading. {{diagram:mavlink-mission-seq Mission upload: the vehicle requests items one at a time and re-sends the request itself on a loss; it finishes with MISSION_ACK.}} Telemetry streams The vehicle sends telemetry either according to its own settings ArduPilot — stream groups per port, SRn_ parameters in 4.6 and MAVn_ in 4.7+; PX4 — MAV_n_MODE profiles , or on the client's request: - MAV_CMD_SET_MESSAGE_INTERVAL 511 : param1 — msgid, param2 — interval in µs −1 — off, 0 — default . - MAV_CMD_REQUEST_MESSAGE 512 : one message now for example, AUTOPILOT_VERSION , HOME_POSITION . Link budget: SiK at 57600 gives ~5 KB/s of payload; ATTITUDE 28 bytes payload + 12 overhead at 10 Hz is 0.4 KB/s. A companion over UART at 921600

headings: Layers MAVSDK: how it works Async without surprises Offboard and GUIDED What happens on a link loss Step 1. One mission, two tools Step 2. Mission flight with progress Step 3. Offboard square Step 4. Link drop
text: summary After four “on the wire” modules you can choose a tool deliberately. pymavlink is direct access to every message; MAVSDK gives you ready-made actions arm , takeoff , mission.upload , offboard on top of the same microservices, an asynchronous API and a C++ server; MAVROS is a MAVLink ↔ ROS bridge; DroneKit is historical and unmaintained. This module compares them by layer, shows the same mission in pymavlink and MAVSDK, takes apart MAVSDK's asynchronous model subscriptions, cancellation, timeouts and what happens on a link loss at each level. Lab: a mission and an offboard flight through MAVSDK in SITL, checking the behavior when the link drops. theory Layers Layer What it gives you What it doesn't When to use it --- --- --- --- Raw protocol mav-protocol everything nothing ready-made a driver on an MCU, your own dialect, debugging pymavlink codec, connections, recv_match , tlog the dialogue logic missions, ACK, retries — on you scripts, log analysis, tests, non-standard messages MAVSDK C++, Python, … actions and microservices: action, telemetry, mission, offboard, param, ftp, camera, gimbal exotic firmware messages possible through mavlink_passthrough companion applications, automated flight tests MAVROS MAVLink ↔ ROS 1/2 topics/services, TF, setpoints ROS independence; overhead a ROS-based system with ArduPilot; for PX4 + ROS 2, uXRCE-DDS is preferred the px4-ros2 module DroneKit-Python — not developed, problems with modern Python and firmware reading old code only All the upper layers implement the same dialogues you wrote by hand: mission.upload_mission is, inside, MISSION_COUNT/REQUEST_INT/ITEM_INT/ACK with retries. You need to understand the lower layer to read the tlog when the upper layer says “timeout.” MAVSDK: how it works MAVSDK is a C++ core; the mavsdk Python package starts a bundled mavsdk_server gRPC and talks to it. Hence: 1 the API is asynchronous asyncio ; 2 telemetry streams are async generators; 3 errors are exceptions with the plugin's result code ActionError , MissionError — the same meaning as MAV_RESULT . python import asyncio from mavsdk import System from mavsdk.mission import MissionItem, MissionPlan async def main : drone = System await drone.connect system_address="udpin://0.0.0.0:14540" older releases: "udp://:14540" async for state in drone.core.connection_state : if state.is_connected: break async for health in drone.telemetry.health : if health.is_global_position_ok and health.is_home_position_ok: break items = MissionItem lat, lon, 20, 5, True, float "nan" , float "nan" , MissionItem.CameraAction.NONE, float "nan" , float "nan" , float "nan" , float "nan" , float "nan" , MissionItem.VehicleAction.NONE for lat, lon in 47.3978, 8.5456 , 47.3982, 8.5460 , 47.3980, 8.5465 await drone.mission.upload_mission MissionPlan items await drone.action.arm await drone.mission.start_mission async for p in drone.mission.mission_progress : print f"{p.current}/{p.total}" if p.current == p.total: break await drone.action.return_to_launch asyncio.run main The MissionItem constructor changes between MAVSDK versions fields get added — check the documentation for the version you have installed; that's the normal price of a high-level API. Async without surprises - Subscriptions are endless : async for x in telemetry.position won't end on its own. The way out is a break on a condition, or a separate task that you cancel. - Timeouts are your job : “wait until GPS is ok” without asyncio.wait_for ..., timeout will hang forever on a vehicle without GPS. - Parallel tasks : telemetry, logging and control are separate asyncio.create_task s; an error in a task whose result is never await ed is lost silently. - One system — one owner : two MAVSDK processes on the same port mean two mavsdk_servers with the same identifiers; separate them with a router and different compids. Offboard and GUIDED High-level control from the companion: in PX4 — Offboard mode MAVSDK offboard.set_velocity_ned ... , then offboard.start ; setpoints must be sent continuously at 2 Hz, otherwise PX4 exits Offboard on timeout , in ArduPilot — GUIDED with SET_POSITION_TARGET_LOCAL_NED MAVSDK offboard also works with ArduPilot through the same messages; support for the set of fields may differ . The safety rule from the comp-intro module: the companion advises, the autopilot decides; if the companion goes silent, the vehicle must switch to safe behavior on its own — and this is verified by a test, not by faith. What happens on a link loss Level Behavior --- --- pymavlink recv_match returns None on timeout; the decision is yours MAVSDK connection_state → is_connected = False on loss of heartbeat, ~3 s ; actions fail with an error; offboard setpoints don't get through Autopilot GCS failsafe if enabled and the link is with the GCS , exit from Offboard/GUIDED on setpoint timeout PX4 COM_OF_LOSS_T , ArduPilot — GUID_TIMEOUT for velocity/acceleration setpoints Design it so that safety is provided by the lower level the autopilot , and the upper level only restores operation. {{diagram:mav-sdk-layers pymavlink, MAVSDK and MAVROS are different levels of abstraction over the same MAVLink.}} practice Step 1. One mission, two tools Upload the same 5-waypoint mission to PX4 SITL or ArduPilot SITL twice: with your own client from mav-services pymavlink and through MAVSDK. Record a tlog of both sessions MAVProxy or mavlink-router and compare the message sequences: what does MAVSDK send in addition version requests, intervals, MISSION_CLEAR_ALL ? Step 2. Mission flight with progress The script above: arm, mission, progress, RTL. Add timeouts to every wait and CSV telemetry recording in a separate task. Step 3. Offboard square NED velocities for 5 s in each of four directions in Offboard PX4 or GUIDED ArduPilot . Then “kill” the script in the middle of the square kill -9 and record from the log how long it took and which mode the autopilot switched to. Compare with the value of the timeout parameter. Step 4. Link drop Between S

text: summary The ESP32 is the perfect “little companion”: UART, Wi-Fi, BLE, a display, a dirt-cheap price and boot in a fraction of a second. This module covers three typical roles: onboard peripherals sensors, indication , a Wi-Fi ↔ FC MAVLink bridge, and a radio companion. The last one is shown on a project for the RadioMaster TX16S: an ESP32-S3 with a screen that shows telemetry in flight and brings up an access point for setup from a phone on the ground. The traps covered: the EdgeTX Lua widget lifecycle, UART levels, the power budget and a verifiable radio shutdown. theory Three roles of the ESP32 1. Onboard peripherals. Polling sensors over I2C, addressable LEDs, servos, relays. The link to the FC goes over UART via MAVLink or a simple text protocol. 2. MAVLink bridge. The ESP32 receives MAVLink over UART from the FC and serves it over Wi-Fi UDP to a phone or laptop. Many off-the-shelf Wi-Fi telemetry modules work this way; your own version is a few dozen lines. 3. Radio companion. The ESP32 is connected to the AUX port of an EdgeTX radio, a Lua script on the radio sends it the state mode, arm, telemetry , and the ESP32 shows it on its own display and provides a settings interface. UART: levels and wires The ESP32 runs at 3.3 V. Flight controllers and EdgeTX radios are also 3.3 V on UART, but check with a multimeter before connecting. The wires are crossed over, and a common GND is mandatory. The baud rate with the radio is whatever is set in the port settings, usually 115200. EdgeTX: the AUX port and Lua In the radio settings Hardware , the AUX1/AUX2 ports have a “Lua” mode: scripts then get access to the functions serialWrite str , serialRead num and setSerialBaudrate baudrate . serialRead with no argument reads up to the first newline, so a “one line = one message” string protocol fits it naturally. Trap: the widget lifecycle An EdgeTX widget has two functions: refresh is called when the widget is visible on the screen, background when it is hidden. If you put the heartbeat send only in refresh , the companion loses the link as soon as the pilot switches screens. The fix: a shared tick function that both of them call. Safe by default A design decision of the project: undefined state = FLIGHT mode, Wi-Fi off. The access point comes up only when the ESP32 has received an explicit “disarmed” from the radio. Every settings write goes through two steps: STAGE prepare → APPLY apply with an automatic backup , and the in-flight write protection is duplicated on both sides — in Lua and in the ESP32 firmware. Turning the radio off must be verifiable: WiFi.mode WIFI_OFF plus esp_wifi_stop , not the assumption “we never turned it on”. Power An ESP32-S3 with active Wi-Fi draws peaks of hundreds of milliamps. From the radio battery or a BEC that is noticeable; in FLIGHT mode with the radio off it is several times less. The budget is calculated per mode, not from the average. A minimal MAVLink bridge on the ESP32 the code idea UART2 Serial2.begin 921600, SERIAL_8N1, RX_PIN, TX_PIN ↔ WiFi UDP: everything that comes from the FC goes to UDP at the last client's address or broadcast 14550 ; everything that comes over UDP goes to UART. 1 KB buffers, no MAVLink parsing the bridge is transparent ; a task on the second FreeRTOS core the “Embedded” module : core 0 is the Wi-Fi stack, core 1 is the UART copying with a priority above loop . The latency of such a bridge is a few ms; losses happen when Wi-Fi is overloaded 2.4 GHz shares the air with ELRS 2.4 — onboard, a Wi-Fi bridge only makes sense for setup on the ground; turn it off in flight . An onboard sensor over MAVLink The ESP32 as a system component: it sends HEARTBEAT its own component_id: MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL 158 or one from the USER1–USER75 range 25–99 , data as NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT / NAMED_VALUE_INT visible in the GCS and in the NVAL log , or DISTANCE_SENSOR 132 for your own rangefinder — ArduPilot accepts it as RNGFND1_TYPE = 10 MAVLink and uses it in the EKF/landing. Library: the mavlink C headers from the generator common.xml , 100 KB of flash , or a minimal hand-written frame builder with CRC the “MAVLink protocols” module . Worked example: a radio companion the TX16S project The line protocol: radio → ESP32 S,<mode ,<armed ,<vbat ,<rssi \n every 500 ms; ESP32 → radio A,<cmd ,<arg \n . ESP32 states: FLIGHT radio off; the default and on a line timeout 2 s → GROUND the radio sent armed=0 for ≥ 3 s in a row: Wi-Fi AP, web settings → FLIGHT on any armed=1 . Settings: STAGE JSON in RAM → APPLY NVS write with a copy of the previous version only in GROUND; the Lua on the radio blocks APPLY if telemetry shows armed. title: Embedded: interrupts, timers, DMA, RTOS
summary: An STM32 flight controller polls the gyro 8000 times per second, computes the PID, sends DShot to four ESCs, receives CRSF, writes a log and draws the OSD — on a single core. This is only possible because the hardware does work without the CPU (DMA, timers), and events arrive as interrupts. This mod
headings: What keeps the flight controller CPU busy Interrupts Timers DMA RTOS: tasks, priorities, queues Jitter and blocking Watchdog Step 1. Two tasks and a queue (ESP32, ESP-IDF or Arduino-FreeRTOS) Step 2. Jitter Step 3. Break it and fix it Step 4. Read the firmware
text: summary An STM32 flight controller polls the gyro 8000 times per second, computes the PID, sends DShot to four ESCs, receives CRSF, writes a log and draws the OSD — on a single core. This is only possible because the hardware does work without the CPU DMA, timers , and events arrive as interrupts. This module explains these mechanisms at the level you need to read firmware and write your own devices: interrupts and priorities, timers and capture/generation, DMA, the Betaflight scheduler, FreeRTOS on the ESP32 and NuttX in PX4, jitter, and why a delay in the loop is a disaster. The ESP32 lab: two FreeRTOS tasks, a queue, a hardware timer, a jitter measurement, a blocking call — shown and eliminated. theory What keeps the flight controller CPU busy The budget at 8 kHz is 125 µs per cycle. A gyro on SPI at 8+ MHz reads 14 bytes in ~15 µs — if you wait in a loop; with DMA it's 0 µs of CPU time. The PID on three axes on an F4 168 MHz takes ~10–20 µs, the filters as much again, DShot goes via timer+DMA 0 µs , CRSF via UART with an interrupt/DMA. The remainder is for lower tasks src/main/fc/tasks.c : TASK_RX — event-driven on frame arrival with a 33 Hz fallback period, TASK_SERIAL 100 Hz, TASK_BATTERY_CURRENT 50 Hz, TASK_OSD per osd framerate_hz , TASK_GPS depending on the port speed, blackbox — on a divider from the PID loop. Betaflight is a cooperative scheduler without an RTOS scheduler.c : every task has a desired period, a priority and a time estimate; the critical tasks gyro/PID don't preempt anything — the scheduler simply doesn't start a lower task if its execution time estimate anticipatedExecutionTime doesn't fit before the next gyro cycle; the rest wait for a “gap”. Interrupts An interrupt is a hardware signal that suspends the current code and calls a handler ISR . Sources: a UART byte is ready, a DMA transfer has completed, a timer fired, an edge on a pin EXTI — that's how the gyro reports “data ready”, Betaflight gyro_sync via EXTI . ISR rules: short microseconds , no blocking calls and no printf , no memory allocation; heavy work goes to a task via a flag/queue. Priorities the NVIC on Cortex-M : an interrupt with a higher priority preempts an ISR with a lower one; the gyro/DShot are higher, the UART log is lower. On the ESP32 — ESP_INTR_FLAG_LEVEL1..3 , the ISR in IRAM IRAM_ATTR , to the other core via a queue. Timers A counter that ticks from the bus and can: generate an interrupt every period the scheduler, periodic tasks , PWM compare , capture an input edge input capture — measuring the pulse width of a PWM receiver , trigger DMA on an event DShot: a timer + DMA writes a sequence of durations into the compare register — that's how a 16-bit DShot frame goes out without the CPU's involvement . The resolution is the timer clock: at 84 MHz it's 12 ns. DMA The direct memory access controller copies data peripheral ↔ memory on events without the CPU: UART reception into a ring buffer, reading the SPI gyro, DShot output, writing to the SD card. Limitations: the number of channels/streams and their binding to peripherals on the STM32F4, DMA stream conflicts are the real reason why some boards can't run DShot on all motors and, say, an LED strip at the same time — that's exactly what the Betaflight target files describe , cache coherency on F7/H7 buffers in non-cacheable memory or SCB_Clean/InvalidateDCache . RTOS: tasks, priorities, queues FreeRTOS ESP32; PX4 runs on NuttX — a different RTOS with the same concepts of tasks, priorities and queues : tasks with priorities and their own stack; a preemptive scheduler — a higher-priority task always gets the core when it's ready; equal ones share by time the tick is 100 Hz by default in ESP-IDF, CONFIG_FREERTOS_HZ ; 1000 Hz in Arduino-ESP32 . Primitives: the queue ISR → task, task → task, copies data, thread-safe , the semaphore/notification an “event” signal , the mutex protecting a shared resource — the I2C bus , the timer software, in the daemon context — not for precise periods . A precise period: vTaskDelayUntil a fixed period from the last wake-up, not from the end of the work or a hardware timer + a notification. Jitter and blocking Jitter is the spread of the actual period. Causes: an ISR doing long work, a higher-priority task, cache misses, delay /waiting in a loop busy-wait , logging with printf from a critical task, flash operations on the ESP32 a flash write halts execution of code from flash on the other core unless it's in IRAM . The norm for a control loop: jitter < 5–10% of the period; PX4 and Betaflight measure and log it DEBUG_CYCLETIME , PX4 perf . Why blocking in the loop is a disaster : the control task waits for the UART for 50 ms → 400 missed cycles at 8 kHz → the gyro data is stale, the D-term jumps, the motors “twitch”; in the worst case the watchdog reboots the controller in flight. Hence the rule: the control loop waits for nothing — it only reads data that is ready. Watchdog A hardware timer that reboots the MCU if it isn't “fed”. Betaflight/ArduPilot/PX4 use it: a hang = a reboot better than an eternal “motors stuck at the last value” ; ArduPilot writes the reason to WDOG / BRD_OPTIONS . On the ESP32 there's the task watchdog on the idle tasks: a task without vTaskDelay blocks idle → the TWDT fires. {{diagram:fc-loop-125us One 8 kHz cycle: gyro read via DMA, filters, PID and mixer, a DShot frame via DMA; a UART interrupt squeezes in, the rest of the cycle goes to slow tasks orders of magnitude, not an exact profile .}} practice Step 1. Two tasks and a queue ESP32, ESP-IDF or Arduino-FreeRTOS c // sensor task: hardware timer notifies every 1 ms; reads IMU or fakes it and pushes a sample static QueueHandle_t q; static TaskHandle_t sensorTask; static void IRAM_ATTR on_timer void arg { // ISR: just notify BaseType_t hp = pdFALSE; vTaskNotifyGiveFromISR sensorTask, &hp ; if hp portYIELD_FROM_ISR ; } static void sensor_task void arg { int64_t last = esp_timer_get_time ; for ;; { ulTaskNotifyTake pdTRUE, portMAX_DELA

text: summary The “Connecting peripherals” module taught you to hook up ready-made parts; this one teaches you to build your own: what bits look like on the wire, why there is a start bit and an ACK, where framing errors and NACKs come from, how timings are calculated and why bus length is limited, and how to write a sensor driver from scratch an I2C barometer/IMU on an ESP32: registers, block reads, error handling, timeouts . It ends with DroneCAN: CAN 2.0 frames, arbitration, node ID, why big aircraft need it and what a DroneCAN packet looks like in an analyzer. theory UART Asynchronous: there is no clock line, both sides know the baud rate. Frame: a start bit 0 , 5–9 data bits LSB first , optional parity, 1–2 stop bits 1 . 8N1 at 115200 → 10 bits per byte → 11,520 bytes/s. The receiver samples in the middle of the bit usually ×16 oversampling ; a baud-rate error of up to ~3–5% is tolerable, more than that gives a framing error . Errors: framing stop bit is not 1 — wrong baud rate/inversion , overrun the byte was not picked up in time — you need DMA/an interrupt , noise. Inversion SBUS : levels are flipped, idle = 0. Levels are 3.3 V TTL; RS-232/RS-485 use other levels/a differential pair long lines . Driver: a receive ring buffer filled by an interrupt/DMA, a protocol frame parser CRSF: address length type payload CRC8 0xD5 ; MAVLink: magic 0xFD, length, seq, sysid/compid, msgid, CRC16 with CRC_EXTRA , an inter-byte timeout for resynchronization. I2C Synchronous, two open-drain lines with pull-ups: SCL, SDA. The master generates the clock; a transaction: START SDA↓ while SCL=1 → 7-bit address + R/W bit → ACK from the slave SDA↓ on the 9th clock → data bytes with ACK/NACK → STOP. Register read: START, address+W, register number, repeated START , address+R, data, NACK on the last byte, STOP. Speeds 100/400 kHz fast , 1 MHz fast-plus . Limits: bus capacitance ≤ 400 pF → wires up to ~30–50 cm, pull-ups 2.2–4.7 kΩ lower — steeper edges, more current . Errors: NACK on the address no device/wrong address/no power , NACK on data, a stuck bus the slave holds SDA=0 after a master glitch — cured by clocking SCL 9 times manually, “bus recovery” , clock stretching the slave holds SCL low — the master must be able to wait; some MCUs/sensors have trouble with it . {{diagram:i2c-transaction Reading a register over I2C: address with the write bit, register address, repeated start, address with the read bit, data.}} SPI Synchronous, full duplex: SCLK, MOSI, MISO, CS one line per device . No addresses and no ACK: the master pulls CS low, outputs clocks, and every clock shifts a bit in both directions. CPOL/CPHA modes 0–3 — clock polarity/phase, must match the datasheet ICM42688 — mode 0 or 3 . Speeds up to tens of MHz gyro 8–24 MHz, flash 50+ . Register read: an address byte with the R bit often the MSB = 1 , then N garbage bytes on MOSI — the data comes back on MISO. A 14-byte IMU burst read in a single transaction — that is how every firmware does it. There are no “protocol” errors — integrity is checked only by meaning the WHO_AM_I register, values within range . Short traces: SPI is almost never routed off the board. CAN and DroneCAN CAN 2.0: a differential pair CAN_H/CAN_L, 120 Ω terminators at both ends, up to 1 Mbit/s up to 40 m at 1 Mbit, longer — slower . Frame: an 11- or 29-bit extended identifier, DLC, up to 8 data bytes, CRC15, ACK from any receiver. Arbitration : everyone transmits at once, a dominant 0 beats a recessive 1 — the lower ID wins with no time lost; priority is built into the ID. The CAN controller in the MCU receives/sends frames in hardware and filters by ID; errors are counted error passive/bus-off at 256 errors — the node disconnects itself . DroneCAN formerly UAVCAN v0 : on top of CAN — a 29-bit ID with priority, message type and source node ID 1–127 , multi-frame messages with a transfer CRC and a toggle bit, dynamic node ID allocation DNA , standard types: uavcan.equipment.gnss.Fix2 , ahrs.MagneticFieldStrength2 , esc.RawCommand/Status , power.BatteryInfo , range_sensor.Measurement . Why on big aircraft: one twisted pair for all devices, the noise immunity of a differential pair and CRC, telemetry from every ESC, hot-swapping nodes, long lines a 2 m wing , no more “one UART — one device”. Tool: DroneCAN GUI Tool an SLCAN adapter or the flight controller as a bridge via CAN_SLCAN_CPORT — you see the nodes, node parameters, messages. Driver: what it must have 1. Bus initialization and a device check WHO_AM_I/chip id . 2. Configuration registers : range, rate, filters. 3. Block reads with a timeout; return an error, never hang. 4. Conversion of raw units to physical ones LSB → °/s, Pa . 5. Error handling: counters, re-initialization after N errors in a row, bus recovery for I2C. 6. Thread safety: a mutex on the bus if there are several devices. practice Step 1. An I2C sensor driver ESP32, ESP-IDF; the example uses the legacy driver/i2c.h API, which is declared end-of-life as of ESP-IDF v6.0 — new projects use driver/i2c_master.h : i2c_master_transmit_receive / i2c_master_transmit Example for the BMP280 address 0x76/0x77, chip id 0x58 in register 0xD0 : c static esp_err_t rd uint8_t reg, uint8_t buf, size_t n { // repeated-START read, 50 ms timeout return i2c_master_write_read_device I2C_NUM_0, ADDR, &reg, 1, buf, n, pdMS_TO_TICKS 50 ; } static esp_err_t wr uint8_t reg, uint8_t val { uint8_t b 2 = { reg, val }; return i2c_master_write_to_device I2C_NUM_0, ADDR, b, 2, pdMS_TO_TICKS 50 ; } esp_err_t bmp280_init void { uint8_t id; ESP_RETURN_ON_ERROR rd 0xD0, &id, 1 , TAG, "no response" ; if id != 0x58 return ESP_ERR_NOT_FOUND; ESP_RETURN_ON_ERROR rd 0x88, calib, 24 , TAG, "calib" ; // dig_T1..dig_P9 return wr 0xF4, 0x57 ; // osrs_t x2, osrs_p x16, normal mode } esp_err_t bmp280_read float temp_c, float press_pa { uint8_t d 6 ; esp_err_t e = rd 0xF7, d, 6 ; if e != ESP_OK { errors++; return e; } int32_t adc_p = d 0 << 12 d 1 << 4 d 2 4 , adc_t = d 3 << 12 d 4 << 4 d 5 4 ; / compensati

text: summary An onboard Raspberry Pi is the classic first companion: Linux, Python, a camera, Wi-Fi. This module takes you from the wire to a working service: connecting to an ArduPilot telemetry port, setting up the UART on the Pi, checking with MAVProxy, routing MAVLink to several consumers at once, the power budget and throttling control, protecting the SD card from power loss, and your own script as a system service with a watchdog timer. theory Wiring The FC telemetry port for example TELEM2 = SERIAL2 ↔ the Pi UART: TX → RX, RX → TX, common GND. 3.3 V levels on both sides. On the FC: - SERIAL2_PROTOCOL = 2 — MAVLink 2; - SERIAL2_BAUD = 921 — 921600 baud; for short wires and a heavy telemetry stream this is normal, for long ones use 57 57600 . Power the Pi from a separate 5 V BEC with current headroom a Pi 4/5 under load draws more than an amp , not from the FC telemetry port. UART on the Raspberry Pi By default the UART is taken by the Linux console. In raspi-config → Interfacing → Serial: login shell over serial — no , hardware port — yes . After a reboot the port is available as /dev/serial0 — that's on the Pi 3/4. On the Pi 5 /dev/serial0 points to the debug connector /dev/ttyAMA10 , while the UART on GPIO 14/15 is enabled with the line dtparam=uart0=on in /boot/firmware/config.txt and is called /dev/ttyAMA0 — substitute it in the examples below. On the Pi 3/4 the main UART is given to Bluetooth by default, and the GPIO gets the mini-UART, whose baud rate “floats” with the core clock: for a stable 921600 use enable_uart=1 and dtoverlay=disable-bt in config.txt . Routing One UART, but several consumers: the GCS over Wi-Fi, your script, tlog recording. The solution is a MAVLink router: mavlink-router or mavp2p reads the port and serves it over UDP/TCP to everyone connected. Scripts then connect to a local UDP port rather than to /dev/serial0 directly, and don't get in each other's way. {{diagram:mavlink-routing mavlink-router serves one FC UART stream to several consumers: the GCS, your scripts and a logger.}} A service instead of “I started it by hand” A script started from a terminal over SSH dies with the session. Onboard, everything must start by itself: a systemd unit with Restart=always . Logs go to journalctl . Time and logs A Pi without a network has no accurate time after boot. To match companion logs with the FC DataFlash, use SYSTEM_TIME from MAVLink GPS time or write TimeUS -like monotonic counter stamps and the moment of synchronization to the log. Power: a budget, not “some BEC” The Raspberry Pi 5 is rated for 5.1 V / 5 A 27 W : idle it draws about 3 W, under full CPU load 7–8 W, plus the camera, a USB modem or a Wi-Fi adapter on top. An example budget: Consumer Power Current at 5 V --- --- --- Pi 5 under load 8 W 1.6 A CSI camera 1.5 W 0.3 A USB Wi-Fi / LTE modem 2.5 W 0.5 A Total 12 W 2.4 A Pick the BEC with at least one and a half to two times headroom 5 A , and the wire short and thick: 30 cm of a 22 AWG pair ≈ 53 mΩ/m per conductor, out and back ≈ 32 mΩ loses ≈ 0.08 V at 2.4 A. Peak surges camera start, modem transmission sag the voltage more than the average — so you need at least ~4.9 V at the Pi connector under load. Overheating and voltage sag show up in numbers vcgencmd get_throttled returns a bitmask: bit 0 — undervoltage right now, 1 — frequency capped, 2 — throttling, 3 — soft temperature limit; bits 16–19 — the same, “has occurred since boot”. 0x0 — all good, 0x50000 — there was undervoltage and throttling; 0x50005 — it's happening right now. Temperature — vcgencmd measure_temp ; without a heatsink and airflow a Pi 5 under load starts throttling within minutes, and even more so inside a drone body with no airflow. A vision algorithm that “suddenly got slower in flight” is almost always this. Power loss without a broken SD card On a drone the power disappears without a shutdown — after a crash, when swapping batteries. A write at the moment of power loss corrupts the SD card's file system. Two approaches that work: - Overlay File System raspi-config → Performance Options → Overlay File System : the root is read-only, changes live in RAM and vanish after a reboot. The system is unkillable, but logs and records have to be written to a separate partition or a USB drive. - Writing like a grown-up : logs on a separate partition or a USB SSD, f.flush + os.fsync for anything important, the systemd journal in RAM Storage=volatile in /etc/systemd/journald.conf so it doesn't wear out the card. A service with a watchdog timer A script started from a terminal over SSH dies with the session. Onboard, everything starts by itself: a systemd unit with Restart=always . If the script can hang rather than crash a socket, the camera, an infinite loop , you also need a watchdog timer: Type=notify and WatchdogSec= — systemd restarts the service if it stops reporting “I'm alive”. Without messages from the script, WatchdogSec simply kills it every N seconds — almost everyone falls into this trap. A working version is in the practice section, step 3. Time and logs A Pi without an RTC and without a network boots into 1970 — absolute timestamps before synchronization are meaningless. The practical way: at startup the script writes a pair SYSTEM_TIME.time_unix_usec from MAVLink — the GPS time from the flight controller, and its own time.monotonic and then uses monotonic stamps; during analysis the companion logs are matched to the flight controller's DataFlash using this pair. The Pi 5 has an RTC battery connector — with a battery the time survives a reboot without a network. practice Step 1. The port and a check sudo raspi-config Interfacing Options - Serial: console NO, hardware YES sudo reboot pip install --user pymavlink MAVProxy mavproxy.py --master=/dev/serial0 --baudrate 921600 If you see the heartbeat and the parameters, the link works. Give the arm throttle command on the bench only with the props off. Step 2. The router An example mavlink-router configuration /etc/mavlink-route

title: MAVLink routing and transport: radio, 4G, multiple GCSs
summary: As soon as more than one participant is connected to a vehicle — a GCS over radio, a companion, a second GCS over 4G, a camera — the question comes up of who receives which packets. MAVLink has no “network layer”: routing relies on sysid/compid conventions and on tables that each node builds from th
headings: Addressing: sysid and compid Forwarding rules (as in ArduPilot) Tools Transports Link metrics and how to measure them Link security Step 1. A router with three clients Step 2. RTT and loss under netem Step 3. UDP vs TCP Step 4. Your system's layout
text: summary As soon as more than one participant is connected to a vehicle — a GCS over radio, a companion, a second GCS over 4G, a camera — the question comes up of who receives which packets. MAVLink has no “network layer”: routing relies on sysid/compid conventions and on tables that each node builds from the packets it has seen. This module goes through these rules using the ArduPilot source code, the tools mavlink-router, MAVProxy, mavp2p , the transports UART, UDP, TCP, SiK radio, 4G/LTE through NAT and VPN , and the link metrics — latency, loss, jitter — measuring them under artificial impairment with tc netem . Lab: a router with three clients and a heartbeat RTT measurement as the network degrades. theory Addressing: sysid and compid - sysid — a vehicle or a station. Vehicles: 1…250 unique on one network! , the GCS is usually 255 a second one — 254 and so on . - compid — a component within a system: autopilot 1, cameras 100–105, gimbal 154, onboard computer 191–194, peripherals 158, GCS application 190. Your own script on the companion gets its own compid in the same system as the autopilot. - A message can have target_system / target_component fields addressed or not have them telemetry — broadcast by nature . target 0 means “everyone.” Forwarding rules as in ArduPilot The source file libraries/GCS_MAVLink/MAVLink_routing.cpp states the rules explicitly. The autopilot handles a packet itself if it has no target, has target_system 0, or is addressed to it. And it forwards it to another port if: 1. the message has no target_system, or target_system = 0; 2. target_system is someone else's, and packets from that sysid have already been seen on that port; 3. target_system is its own, there is a target_component, and packets from that sysid/compid pair have already been seen on that port. Consequences you need to know by heart: - A route appears only after the first packet from the addressee. A script on the companion that stays silent won't receive a single addressed command from the GCS — let it send its own heartbeat. - A packet is never sent back to the port it came in on. - The routing table is reset on reboot; the GCS must notice time_boot_ms decreasing in SYSTEM_TIME and relearn the routes. - A port can be excluded from forwarding: in ArduPilot 4.7+ — MAVn_OPTIONS bit 1 “Don't forward mavlink to/from,” in 4.6 and earlier — SERIALn_OPTIONS bit 10. You need this, for example, for a port with a “chatty” device on it. {{diagram:mavlink-topology Typical topology: the autopilot and the companion router connect the GCS over radio and over 4G to the onboard components.}} Tools - mavlink-router C++, a systemd service : one or more UARTs + UDP/TCP endpoints, routing by the same rules, filtering by msgid, tlog recording. The standard for Raspberry Pi/Jetson; configuration is in the comp-raspberry module. - MAVProxy Python : both a router --out and a console GCS with modules. Handy for debugging, heavier for permanent onboard use. - mavp2p Go : a lightweight router for the same purpose, a single binary. - In the autopilot itself: every SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 MAVLink2 port takes part in forwarding. Sometimes you don't need the companion as a router at all — two autopilot ports are enough. Transports Transport Latency Loss Notes --- --- --- --- UART to the companion < 1 ms ~0 921600 baud ≈ 90 KB/s; needs a common GND and 3.3 V levels SiK radio 433/868/915 30–100 ms 0–10 % air rate 64 kbit/s by default, half-duplex TDM; RADIO_STATUS 109 with RSSI/noise/free buffer space txbuf ; ECC halves the throughput ELRS/Crossfire MAVLink 10–50 ms depends on rate telemetry shares the air with control — a narrow channel Wi-Fi 2–20 ms bursts range of hundreds of meters; UDP broadcast is convenient but noisy 4G/LTE 50–300 ms, jitter 0–5 %, dropouts the modem has a private IP behind the carrier's NAT: no incoming connections NAT and 4G. A vehicle behind NAT can't accept incoming connections. Options: 1 a VPN — WireGuard/Tailscale/ZeroTier, the vehicle and GCS get addresses on the same virtual network; 2 a relay server with a public IP that both connect to mavlink-router in TCP server mode on a VPS ; 3 cloud services. A VPN also encrypts — which MAVLink signing doesn't do. For MAVLink over IP, UDP is preferable: under loss TCP retransmits old data and gives you “telemetry from the past” with delays of seconds. Link metrics and how to measure them - RTT — from sending to the reply: TIMESYNC or MAV_CMD_REQUEST_MESSAGE /reply, or a heartbeat echo via your own message. Median and 95th percentile, not the mean. - Loss — from gaps in seq the mav-protocol module and from RADIO_STATUS.rxerrors . - Jitter — the spread of intervals between packets of a stream with a nominal rate. - Throughput — the sum of frame sizes per second; compare it with the link budget. You can reproduce impairments on Linux without a radio: bash sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem delay 120ms 40ms distribution normal loss 5% ... measurements ... sudo tc qdisc del dev lo root Link security MAVLink signing protects against command spoofing, a VPN against eavesdropping and spoofing on the IP segment, frequency hopping and AES in the radio modem on the radio segment. None of these protect against jamming — failsafe procedures and autonomy protect against that the nav-resilience module . practice Step 1. A router with three clients On your machine: ArduPilot SITL or examples/mavlink/fake_vehicle.py → mavlink-routerd or mavproxy.py --out → three clients: QGC on 14550, your script on 14551, a tlog logger on 14552. Check: a script without its own heartbeat doesn't receive the COMMAND_ACK addressed to it; with a heartbeat, it does. Step 2. RTT and loss under netem Write link_probe.py : every 100 ms it sends TIMESYNC tc1 = 0, ts1 = now_ns , receives the reply, records the RTT; in parallel it counts losses from seq. title: Remote ID and vehicle security: broadcast, MAVLink signing, firmware protection
summary: Два вопроса, которые инженер БПЛА обязан закрыть до серийной эксплуатации: «видит ли регулятор, кто летит» и «может ли посторонний управлять моим аппаратом». Первый — Remote ID: аппарат в полёте транслирует свой идентификатор, координаты и положение пилота, а в ряде стран это обязательное условие по
headings: Remote ID: что передаётся Кому и когда обязательно Remote ID на ArduPilot и PX4 Поверхность атаки Подпись MAVLink 2: как работает Companion: сеть — главная дыра Прошивка и параметры Шаг 1. Карта своего аппарата Шаг 2. Подпись в SITL Шаг 3. Companion Шаг 4. Remote ID (если есть модуль)
text: summary Два вопроса, которые инженер БПЛА обязан закрыть до серийной эксплуатации: «видит ли регулятор, кто летит» и «может ли посторонний управлять моим аппаратом». Первый — Remote ID: аппарат в полёте транслирует свой идентификатор, координаты и положение пилота, а в ряде стран это обязательное условие полётов. Второй — поверхность атаки: RC-линк, телеметрия MAVLink, GNSS, сеть companion-компьютера и сама прошивка. Модуль разбирает, что и как передаёт Remote ID, как его подключают к ArduPilot и PX4, как работает подпись MAVLink 2 и чего она не делает, где открыт companion и как защищают прошивку от подмены. Лабораторная — включить подпись в SITL и доказать, что неподписанные команды отбрасываются. theory Remote ID: что передаётся Remote ID Drone ID — широковещательная трансляция с борта, которую принимает обычный смартфон рядом с аппаратом. По стандарту ASTM F3411 на нём основаны правила США и европейскому стандарту ASD-STAN EN 4709-002 в сообщениях есть: - идентификатор аппарата серийный номер и/или регистрационный номер оператора; - координаты, высота, скорость и курс аппарата; - координаты пульта/пилота или точки взлёта — в зависимости от правил ; - метка времени и статус в том числе аварийный . Транспорт — Bluetooth 4 legacy и 5 long range и Wi-Fi NAN и Beacon . Это широковещание , без связи с сервером, поэтому работает без интернета. Кому и когда обязательно В США — правило FAA Part 89 обязательно для большинства полётов с марта 2024 : встроенный Remote ID, внешний модуль-«маячок» или полёты только в специально отведённых зонах FRIA . В ЕС прямой Remote ID — часть требований к классам C1–C3 и к категории specific, плюс регистрационный номер оператора. В других странах правила свои и меняются — проверяйте у своего авиационного регулятора до первого полёта; модуль f-regulations — отправная точка. Remote ID на ArduPilot и PX4 - Модуль по MAVLink или DroneCAN берёт координаты у автопилота и транслирует их. Готовые модули Cube ID, Holybro и другие с поддержкой OpenDroneID или открытый ArduRemoteID — прошивка ArduPilot для плат ESP32-S3/ESP32-C3, подключаемых по MAVLink или DroneCAN для CAN нужен внешний трансивер . - Отдельный маячок — со своим GPS и батареей; к автопилоту не подключается. - ArduPilot : подсистема OpenDroneID — DID_ENABLE , порт DID_MAVPORT или DID_CANDRIVER , DID_OPTIONS . Для сертифицированных конфигураций используется специальная сборка прошивки с защитой от изменения и проверками перед взлётом: без рабочего Remote ID аппарат не армится. ArduRemoteID умеет блокировать изменение своих параметров изменения — только подписанными командами . - PX4 : поддерживает сообщения OpenDroneID и внешние модули; включение и проверки — по разделу Remote ID документации своей версии. - Сообщения MAVLink: семейство OPEN_DRONE_ID_ OPEN_DRONE_ID_BASIC_ID , _LOCATION , _SYSTEM , _OPERATOR_ID ; координаты пилота на модуль присылает наземка OPEN_DRONE_ID_SYSTEM . Поверхность атаки Канал Угроза Защита --- --- --- RC-линк чужой передатчик с тем же binding, глушение уникальная binding phrase в ELRS это идентификатор пары, не шифрование , продуманный failsafe Телеметрия MAVLink чужие команды: смена режима, disarm, загрузка миссии подпись MAVLink 2, отдельные ключи на аппарат, MAVLink 1 выключен на радиопортах GNSS глушение, спуфинг проверки EKF, навигация без GNSS, оценка по nav-resilience Companion открытый Wi-Fi, пароль по умолчанию, SSH, UDP-телеметрия на весь сегмент, DDS без защиты ключи SSH вместо паролей, файрвол, телеметрия только на нужный адрес, ограничение discovery и SROS2 Прошивка подмена прошивки или параметров подписанная прошивка и защищённый загрузчик, контроль версий параметров Подпись MAVLink 2: как работает - У аппарата и наземки общий секретный ключ 32 байта . К каждому пакету добавляется 13 байт: link ID 1 байт , метка времени 6 байт, в единицах 10 мкс с 1 января 2015 и подпись 6 байт — первые 48 бит SHA-256 от ключа, заголовка, полезной нагрузки, CRC, link ID и метки времени . - Метка времени должна расти — повтор записанного пакета replay отбрасывается. - ArduPilot : на портах MAVLink 2 команды без правильной подписи не исполняются, телеметрия вниз идёт как раньше. USB не защищён — по USB можно сменить или стереть ключ физический доступ = полный доступ . MAVLink 1 подписи не имеет — радиопорты переводят в MAVLink 2 SERIALn_PROTOCOL = 2 . В Mission Planner: Setup → Advanced → MAVLink Signing. - Подпись — это аутентификация, не шифрование. Трафик остаётся читаемым: координаты, миссия и параметры видны любому с приёмником. Шифрование — на уровне радио например, AES в некоторых телеметрийных модемах, ключ в WFB-ng или VPN поверх IP. Companion: сеть — главная дыра - Raspberry Pi или Jetson с паролем по умолчанию, SSH по паролю и точкой доступа Wi-Fi — первое, что найдёт атакующий. - mavlink-router /MAVProxy, вещающие телеметрию на broadcast-адрес, отдают её всем в сети — указывайте конкретный адрес наземки. - ROS 2 по умолчанию ищет участников по multicast во всей сети. ROS_DOMAIN_ID разделяет системы, но не защищает ; в Jazzy ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE=LOCALHOST ограничивает discovery машиной. Аутентификация и шифрование DDS — SROS2 DDS Security . Прошивка и параметры - ArduPilot поддерживает подписанную прошивку : в загрузчик зашивается публичный ключ, прошивка подписывается приватным; неподписанную загрузчик не запустит. Ключ хранится вне репозитория, процедура — по документации Secure Firmware. - Параметры — тоже конфигурация безопасности: хранить эталонный файл параметров в git модуль eng-ci-configs , сравнивать перед полётом. {{diagram:security-surface Каналы атаки на аппарат и их защита: binding и failsafe для RC, подпись MAVLink 2 для телеметрии, проверки EKF для GNSS, файрвол и SROS2 для companion, подписанная прошивка.}} practice Шаг 1. title: Your own MAVLink component: sensor, parameters, messages
summary: Until now the companion was a client: it read telemetry and sent commands. Here it becomes a **member of the system** — a component with its own compid, heartbeat, parameters and messages that the autopilot uses as sensor data. This is how rangefinders, obstacle sensors, external navigation, gimbals
headings: What makes a component “proper” Distance sensor: DISTANCE_SENSOR (132) Obstacles and external navigation Debug messages Python implementation ESP32 implementation (C) Testing the component Step 1. Component tests Step 2. ArduPilot SITL accepts the rangefinder Step 3. A component parameter Step 4. ESP32
text: summary Until now the companion was a client: it read telemetry and sent commands. Here it becomes a member of the system — a component with its own compid, heartbeat, parameters and messages that the autopilot uses as sensor data. This is how rangefinders, obstacle sensors, external navigation, gimbals and payloads connect to ArduPilot and PX4. The module covers the component's duties heartbeat, answering requests, parameters , sensor messages DISTANCE_SENSOR , OBSTACLE_DISTANCE , ODOMETRY / VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE , debug messages NAMED_VALUE_ , DEBUG_VECT , and two implementations: Python on the companion and C on an ESP32. The lab: a virtual rangefinder that ArduPilot SITL accepts as RNGFND1 , then the same component on an ESP32. theory What makes a component “proper” 1. Heartbeat at 1 Hz with its own MAV_TYPE for a sensor — MAV_TYPE_GENERIC or a specific one , MAV_AUTOPILOT_INVALID it is not an autopilot! , the sysid of its own system the same aircraft , a unique compid. Without a heartbeat, routing to the component does not work the mav-routing module . 2. Answers the requests addressed to it : COMMAND_LONG with its compid → COMMAND_ACK even UNSUPPORTED is better than silence, on which the client will hang until it times out ; MAV_CMD_REQUEST_MESSAGE for a COMPONENT_INFORMATION / AUTOPILOT_VERSION -style description — when possible. 3. Its own parameters — if it needs them, via the parameter protocol: it answers PARAM_REQUEST_LIST / PARAM_REQUEST_READ / PARAM_SET from the GCS addressed to its compid; it stores the values in non-volatile memory. QGC and Mission Planner will show them in a separate group for the component. 4. Does not duplicate other components' messages and does not send the autopilot commands that conflict with the operator. 5. Degrades honestly : when measurements are lost, it stops sending the message or sets an invalid flag instead of continuing to report the last value. The autopilot will detect the timeout and disable the source. Distance sensor: DISTANCE_SENSOR 132 Fields: time_boot_ms , min_distance / max_distance / current_distance in centimeters , type MAV_DISTANCE_SENSOR_LASER , _ULTRASOUND , _RADAR … , id , orientation MAV_SENSOR_ROTATION_PITCH_270 = down, _NONE = forward… , covariance 255 — unknown , and in the extension fields — horizontal_fov , vertical_fov , quaternion , signal_quality 0 — unknown, 1 — signal invalid … 100 — excellent . ArduPilot: RNGFND1_TYPE = 10 MAVLink , RNGFND1_ORIENT = 25 down , RNGFND1_MIN / RNGFND1_MAX in meters in new versions, _MIN_CM / _MAX_CM in old ones . The autopilot treats values outside the min, max range as “out of range”, not as a measurement. Rate — 10–50 Hz; the MAVLink rangefinder timeout in ArduPilot is 500 ms: if packets arrive less often than ~2 Hz or with gaps longer than 0.5 s, the sensor is considered lost. A downward rangefinder is used for height above ground RFND in the log, EKF source POSZ = rangefinder, landing, terrain following ; sensors in other orientations — for obstacle avoidance PRX proximity, PRX1_TYPE = 2 MAVLink . Obstacles and external navigation - OBSTACLE_DISTANCE 330 : an array of 72 distances by sector increment degrees per sector, angle_offset , for 2D lidars and stereo cameras → proximity in ArduPilot PRX1_TYPE = 2 , collision prevention in PX4. - VISION_POSITION_ESTIMATE 102 , VISION_SPEED_ESTIMATE 103 , ODOMETRY 331 : pose/velocity from VIO or motion capture → the ArduPilot EKF as ExternalNav EK3_SRC1_POSXY = 6 , PX4 — as vision EKF2_EV_CTRL . What matters here is time usec timestamps, TIMESYNC and coordinate frames FRD/NED versus FLU/ENU — the math-linalg-rot module . Debug messages To show your own value in the GCS and in the log without your own dialect: NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT 251 — a name of up to 10 characters and a float; NAMED_VALUE_INT 252 ; DEBUG_VECT 250 — a name and three floats. Mission Planner shows them in the Quick tab/graphs, ArduPilot writes received NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT to the log NVAL , PX4 — to the ulog as debug topics. For a permanent integration — your own dialect the mav-protocol module or TUNNEL 385 . Python implementation examples/mavlink/virtual_rangefinder.py — the whole component: its own compid MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL , heartbeat, reading GLOBAL_POSITION_INT to simulate a measurement, publishing DISTANCE_SENSOR at a set rate, range limiting. The structure polling, sending at a fixed rate, heartbeat separately is the same for any sensor: replace measurement_cm with reading a real lidar over UART/I2C — and you have a working driver. ESP32 implementation C On a microcontroller you use the generated C library the header-only c_library_v2 or your own from mavgen : c include <common/mavlink.h static void send_distance uart_port_t uart, uint16_t dist_cm { mavlink_message_t msg; uint8_t buf MAVLINK_MAX_PACKET_LEN ; mavlink_msg_distance_sensor_pack 1, MAV_COMP_ID_PERIPHERAL, &msg, esp_timer_get_time / 1000, 20, 4000, dist_cm, MAV_DISTANCE_SENSOR_LASER, 0, MAV_SENSOR_ROTATION_PITCH_270, 255, 0, 0, NULL, 0 ; / fovs, quaternion, signal_quality: extensions / uint16_t len = mavlink_msg_to_send_buffer buf, &msg ; uart_write_bytes uart, const char buf, len ; } Reception — byte by byte via mavlink_parse_char chan, byte, &msg, &status in the task that reads the UART. A separate FreeRTOS task sends a heartbeat once a second; sending from several tasks must be under a mutex, otherwise the frames get mixed up in the UART. ESP-IDF and UART details — the comp-esp32 module. Testing the component A component is tested on three levels: 1 unit — the measurement/packing function test_component.py , range limiting ; 2 integration with a fake vehicle — the message arrived with the right compid and orientation; 3 SITL — the autopilot really uses the data RFND.Dist in the log matches what was sent, RNGFND1 is healthy in the status . Only the third level proves that the autopilot parameters and the message agree. {{diagram:mav-component-seq The minimum for a “proper” component: a HEARTBEAT with

Connection and the component Step 2. Radio Step 3. From companion code Step 4. A mission with ROI and capture Step 5. Center of mass with a payload
text: summary Inspection, mapping, tracking — in every project of the course the camera has to look where the task needs it to, not where the vehicle happens to be pointing. That is the gimbal's job, and these days you talk to it over MAVLink Gimbal Protocol v2. This module covers who is the “manager” and who is the “device” in the system, how to connect a gimbal to ArduPilot MNT1_ and PX4 MNT_ , how to control it from the radio, from a mission and from companion code, how to tie the camera CAM1_ to distance-based image capture, and how not to drop the vehicle along with the released payload — from the center of mass to testing the release mechanism. theory Why a gimbal and which one - Stabilization. A brushless gimbal holds the camera using its own IMU, soaking up vibration and body tilt; the vehicle banks 10–20° in the wind, the picture doesn't. - Pointing. The camera looks at a point ROI independently of the vehicle's heading: orbiting a tower, tracking a target, nadir for mapping. - Types. Servo gimbal two servos, cheap, pointing without stabilization or only rough , brushless gimbal with its own controller SimpleBGC/STorM32 and similar , “smart” gimbal with a built-in camera Siyi, ViewPro, Gremsy and others with its own protocol or MAVLink. Gimbal Protocol v2: manager and device The old protocol MOUNT_CONTROL , DO_MOUNT_CONTROL sent commands straight to the gimbal: the radio, the GCS and the companion fought over who sent the last command. In v2 the roles are separated: - Gimbal device — the gimbal itself: motors, IMU, stabilization. It accepts GIMBAL_DEVICE_SET_ATTITUDE and reports its attitude in GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS quaternion, flags, errors . - Gimbal manager — usually the autopilot. It knows the vehicle's attitude, turns “look at this point” into angles, decides who is in control right now primary/secondary control , and hands commands to the device. - Clients — GCS, companion, mission, radio — send commands to the manager: MAV_CMD_DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_PITCHYAW or a stream of GIMBAL_MANAGER_SET_PITCHYAW , and take control with MAV_CMD_DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_CONFIGURE . The angle flags matter: yaw can be set “relative to the vehicle” follow or “relative to north” lock . To orbit an object you need lock or ROI, otherwise the camera turns along with the vehicle. ArduPilot: MNT1_ What Parameter Comment --- --- --- Gimbal type MNT1_TYPE servo, Brushless PWM, SToRM32, Siyi, ViewPro, Gremsy/MAVLink, etc. — value from the list for your version Default mode MNT1_DEFLT_MODE 0 retract, 1 neutral, 2 MAVLink, 3 RC, 4 GPS point, 5 SysID, 6 Home Limits MNT1_PITCH_MIN/MAX , MNT1_YAW_MIN/MAX , MNT1_ROLL_MIN/MAX gimbal mechanics, in degrees Radio: angle or rate MNT1_RC_RATE 0 — the stick sets the angle, 0 — rate in °/s Radio channels RCx_OPTION 212 Mount1 Roll, 213 Mount1 Pitch, 214 Mount1 Yaw, 163 Mount Lock heading hold Servo gimbal SERVOn_FUNCTION 6 Mount1 Yaw, 7 Mount1 Pitch, 8 Mount1 Roll Smart gimbal port SERIALn_PROTOCOL 8 = Gimbal Siyi, ViewPro, etc. ; for a MAVLink gimbal — MAVLink 2 A MAVLink gimbal has to show up as a separate component MAV_COMP_ID_GIMBAL , 154 — you can see it in the GCS MAVLink inspector. No component — no control. PX4: MNT_ MNT_MODE_IN selects the command source RC, MAVLink Gimbal v1/v2 , MNT_MODE_OUT sets how PX4 drives the gimbal AUX/PWM outputs or MAVLink Gimbal v2 . For a MAVLink gimbal you need a port running MAVLink; servo outputs go through the Actuators tab. Details change between versions — check against the Gimbal Mount section of the PX4 docs. Camera: capture on command and by distance - ArduPilot: CAM1_TYPE — how to fire the shutter servo, relay, via the gimbal, MAVLink, MAVLink Camera v2 . CAM1_TRIGG_DIST or the mission command DO_SET_CAM_TRIGG_DIST — a shot every N meters. Every shot is written to the log CAM with coordinates — that is the basis of georeferencing in mapping. - MAVLink Camera Protocol v2: MAV_CMD_IMAGE_START_CAPTURE , MAV_CMD_VIDEO_START_CAPTURE , with the reply CAMERA_IMAGE_CAPTURED carrying coordinates and the frame index. - Mission: DO_SET_ROI_LOCATION — look at a point, DO_SET_ROI_NONE — release it, DO_GIMBAL_MANAGER_PITCHYAW — set angles; for nadir — pitch −90°. Payload: mass, center of mass, drop - Center of mass. A load under the frame lowers the CoM and shifts it forward/back — the throttle balance between motors changes. Rule: after installing the payload, look at the motor outputs at hover in the log; a spread of more than ~10 % between front and rear means move the payload or the battery. - Mass and tuning. +30 % mass means higher hover throttle and different inertia; check MOT_THST_HOVER ArduPilot after the first flights and, if the difference is noticeable, run autotune with the payload. - Drop. The load leaves — the mass drops in a step, the vehicle “jumps”. Drop with altitude to spare, in a hover, in a mode that holds altitude. ArduPilot: GRIP_ENABLE = 1 , GRIP_TYPE servo or electromagnet , the command MAV_CMD_DO_GRIPPER in a mission or from the radio RCx_OPTION 19 — Gripper . - Payload failure. The gimbal can go into an error state overheating, a jammed motor — flags in GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS . The mission must not depend on the gimbal for flight safety. {{diagram:gimbal-manager Gimbal Protocol v2: clients GCS, companion, radio, mission command the manager in the autopilot; the manager commands the gimbal and receives its attitude back.}} practice Step 1. Connection and the component Connect a gimbal SITL will do: ArduPilot SITL has a simulated gimbal, MNT1_TYPE = 1 with servos or a MAVLink gimbal per the SITL docs . Set MNT1_TYPE and the limits, reboot. In the MAVLink inspector find GIMBAL_DEVICE_ATTITUDE_STATUS for servo and serial gimbals the autopilot itself sends it, component 1; a separate component 154 only appears with a MAVLink gimbal . Write down the message rate. Step 2. Radio RC6_OPTION = 213 pitch , RC8_OPTION = 214 yaw , MNT1_RC_RATE = 0 . Check that the stick sets the angle and the limits are respected.
